items.meaning_mnemonic: A stalk of <radical>grain</radical> leans over on the left, and tucked in behind it on the right is a little <radical>cocoon</radical>, sealed tight. Nobody else knows it is there. You grew the whole crop out in the open, then wrapped one seed away for yourself and told no one. Grain kept back inside a cocoon is what is <radical>private</radical>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Shi is the quiet one who keeps her own small field behind the house, and when anyone asks what she is growing in it she says 「<reading>し</reading>」 and closes the gate. Not rude, exactly. Whatever is in there is hers, and し is the only answer you are ever going to get.

items.mnemonic_text: A single horizontal stroke is the ground floor: one.
items.meaning_mnemonic: One flat line of hard-packed dirt stretches across an empty plain. Standing dead centre on that <radical>ground</radical> is the smug goat — the only creature that matters, in her own mind. Today she holds a talent show: one contestant, one stage, one judge, all her. She awards herself the prize: a mouthful of dirt. One stroke, one goat, one winner: one.
items.reading_mnemonic: The talent show finally gets an audience: a sunburnt hiker named Itchy, with one mosquito bite right between his shoulder blades. He sits on the ground and scratches his back against the goat. Each scrape earns a groan of <reading>いち</reading>, いち, いち.
items.description: Beyond the plain counting number, 一 carries a wider sense of a single thing taken as a whole, so it turns up in words about being first, being the same, or doing something all at once. Write it as one confident horizontal stroke, left to right, and keep it flat and reasonably long — short or slanted, it starts to look like a fragment of some other character.

items.mnemonic_text: Two stacked strokes count out two.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The raccoon is back at the noodle shop table, its broth going cold. Look at 二 and you see its handiwork. One short flat line lies above one longer one — a snapped chopstick above the whole one it came from. A second raccoon slips in, sees the arrangement, and snaps its own chopstick to match. Four paws, nobody eating: <radical>two</radical>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The waiter, Niko, stopped being surprised by raccoons years ago — now he just keeps score. He sets the second bowl beside the first, taps the table once, and says <reading>に</reading>, flat as a bell. It's how you announce a total, not a discovery. The raccoons snap chopsticks purely to hear him say it.
items.description: 二 is the plain counting two, used for quantities, dates, prices and floors. Its spoken form shifts with the counter that follows, so the same character sounds different in a date than in a count of objects. Write it as two level horizontals, top to bottom, the lower one clearly longer — that length difference is the whole character, and the two strokes never touch.

items.mnemonic_text: Three stacked strokes: one, two, three.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Look at this character and count what you see: <radical>three</radical> flat lines stacked neatly on top of each other. One line, then another, then a third. Three lines means, simply, three.
items.reading_mnemonic: A cheerful ranch hand named San lines up three fence rails on the mountain trail, tapping each one and calling out 「<reading>さん</reading>」 as she checks the count. Three rails, three, and San says the number every time.
items.description: The kanji for three, the number 3, appearing constantly in counting, dates, and prices.

items.mnemonic_text: A mouth boxing in legs that kick four ways: four.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You peer into the closed box of the <radical>enclosure</radical>, walls all around, and inside you find a <radical>mouth</radical> trapped in the corner. It sits there counting on its lips, and the number it keeps landing on is four. An enclosure with a mouth inside: four.
items.reading_mnemonic: Inside those walls, a tiny shopkeeper named Shi is stacking exactly four onigiri and hissing "<reading>し</reading>, し, し" as she counts. Every time she runs out of breath, she's counted to four.
items.description: 四 and 西 are both boxes with strokes inside. 四 is a plain rectangle with two short strokes bending inward. 西 sits an extra horizontal bar above the box, which 四 never has.

items.mnemonic_text: A shape crossing itself, the hand held up: five fingers.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Look at this character and picture a hook or a hand reaching sideways to snag things off a shelf. items.reading_mnemonic: The kid counting up his catch is Go, and once he hits five he throws his hands up and yells "<reading>ご</reading>!" like it's the winning number. Every time he lands a fifth thing, out comes that triumphant ご.
items.description: The kanji for five, the number 5, seen everywhere from prices and dates to counting and phone numbers.

items.meaning_mnemonic: A single <radical>step</radical> at the left edge, and beside it a hide being hauled off in one sheet — all <radical>skin</radical>, no animal left. Someone walked past carrying it a moment ago and is already down the road. You never saw the face, only the back of him. That man over there, the one you point at and cannot name: <radical>he</radical>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Hii is the little intake of breath you make when the man in the skin cloak goes past without a word — 「<reading>ひ</reading>」 — and by the time you have finished it he is round the corner. Every single time you catch sight of him: ひ.

items.mnemonic_text: A little hat on two legs stands over six.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the <radical>number eight</radical> standing tall, and then set a little <radical>lid</radical> right on top of it. That lid caps the eight and knocks it down two — from eight, you drop to six. The lid on top of eight always means six.
items.reading_mnemonic: A rock star climbs onto the vending machine at the top of the mountain trail and belts out six songs to the empty air. Every time he screams "<reading>ろく</reading>!" a cat appears, until six of them are yowling backup. That rock (ろく) show is how you hear six.
items.description: Means six; the basic number 6, seen everywhere from counting and prices to dates and times.

items.mnemonic_text: A slanted cross like a scythe cutting seven.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The raccoon is still airborne, still gripping that bent <radical>spoon</radical> — its handle twisted into a crooked hook by the ice cream. items.reading_mnemonic: A shy cat at Grandma Kane's shrine will only come out when you call it exactly seven times — and each time you call, you shush the other cats: <reading>しち</reading>, しち, quiet now. By the seventh しち, it finally pads down the mossy steps.
items.description: 七 and 十 are both a bar crossed by a second stroke. 十 keeps that stroke straight, running top to bottom. 七 bends it: it drops, curves right, and flicks upward at the end.

items.mnemonic_text: Two strokes spreading apart like the number eight opening up.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Look at those two strokes leaning away from each other, spreading apart at the bottom like legs mid-stride. They're <radical>splitting</radical>, opening wider and wider — and the wider they split, the bigger the number gets. That spread lands you on eight.
items.reading_mnemonic: A honeybee — a <reading>はち</reading> in Japanese — drifts down to the onigiri shelf in Koichi's konbini and lands on exactly eight of them, one after another. You count the buzzing little はち as it goes: eight stops, eight onigiri.
items.description: The same two falling strokes, arranged three ways. 八 leaves a clear gap at the top with both strokes leaning apart. 人 joins them into one peak. 入 tucks the short stroke under the long one so the top overhangs.

items.mnemonic_text: A hook curling back at the top of the count: nine.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Look at this character as a hook curling forward — the cane you lean on after a long day. Count the mountain trail's switchbacks, one by one, up to the very last, most brutal bend. That bend curls exactly like this hook. Lean your cane there: that's nine.
items.reading_mnemonic: At bend nine on the mountain trail you finally reach the vending machine, but your legs give out — you go "<reading>きゅう</reading>!" as you collapse against it. That sharp little cry of relief at spot nine is exactly the sound きゅう.
items.description: 九 and 力 are both two strokes with a hook, hooking opposite ways. 九 opens with a short slash, then a stroke that curves right and flicks upward. 力 opens with a flat horizontal that turns down and hooks to the left, with a slash cutting through it.

items.mnemonic_text: A perfect plus sign, fingers of both hands: ten.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Look at this character and you see one perfect plus sign, one clean <radical>cross</radical>. That plus sign is the mark you use when you count all the way up to a full set on your fingers — two hands, all of them raised. A single cross standing tall like this means ten.
items.reading_mnemonic: A judo champion bursts into Koichi's konbini and slaps down exactly ten coins on the beeping till, shouting <reading>じゅう</reading> with each one. Every time you picture that plus-sign cross, hear the judo master's じゅう ringing out.
items.description: 十 is a plain cross: one flat horizontal and one straight vertical. 千 adds a slanting flick above the bar. 七 bends the second stroke instead, curving it right and flicking upward at the end rather than running straight down.

items.mnemonic_text: A window with a line: the sun rising to mark the day.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Look at the character: it's a window with a bar across the middle. Through that window you can see the <radical>sun</radical> climbing into the sky, and once the sun is up, a whole new day begins. Window plus bar, sun in the frame — that's a day.
items.reading_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, one cat wakes at dawn and greets the rising sun with the same cry every morning: "<reading>にち</reading>! にち!" The others answer, and that's how the whole shrine knows a new day has started.
items.description: Check the top and count the bars. 日 is a plain box with one horizontal inside. 白 is the same box with a small flick added on top. 目 has no cap but carries two horizontals instead of one.

items.mnemonic_text: A crescent with two lines: the moon marking each month.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Look up on a clear night and there it is: a thin crescent hanging in the dark, the <radical>moon</radical>. Watch that crescent fatten, fade, and swing back around, and you've just watched one whole month go by. This character is that crescent — so it means moon, and it means month.
items.reading_mnemonic: A gecko has claimed the moon as its own, scuttling across the crescent every night. Whenever it does, you hear its little feet go <reading>げつ</reading>, げつ against the pale surface. That gecko-on-the-moon sound is how you remember げつ.
items.description: Means moon or month; a common kanji that shows up in dates, days of the week (Monday), and countless month-related words.

Dig it up, and you've got gold and money.
items.reading_mnemonic: Grandma Kane keeps her real fortune under the shrine's giant bell, and every time a cat brushes it, it goes <reading>きん</reading>. That soft きん ring is the sound of gold sitting safe underneath.

items.mnemonic_text: Steam rising with an X inside: the invisible energy or mood.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a little puff of <radical>steam</radical> curling up off a hot bowl of rice — that swirling, rising shape is exactly this character. You can almost see the wisp lifting into the air, alive and moving. That invisible thing rising off warm things is the very idea of spirit and energy.
items.reading_mnemonic: The steam curls up and out pops Kiki, the tree spirit, giggling as the wind stirs her branches. She rides that rising energy on a breeze of 「<reading>き</reading>」.
items.description: Means spirit or energy; a very common kanji found in words about mood, feeling, weather, and vitality.

items.mnemonic_text: A mark sitting on top of a line: up and above.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a single flat line of <radical>ground</radical>, and a tortoise standing on it, squinting at the cracks in its shell. items.reading_mnemonic: A cheerful mountaineer plants her flag at the summit and shouts "Joe!" as she looks up at the sky — <reading>じょう</reading> rings out across the peak. Every time you look up and above you, you hear her じょう echoing back down.
items.description: Means "up" or "above"; a very common N5 kanji appearing in words for direction, position, and going up.

example_sentences.english: The teacher is good at speaking.

example_sentences.japanese: 本の上に猫が寝ています。

items.meaning_mnemonic: The tortoise props its hand mirror flat on the level <radical>ground</radical> and squints at the cracks running underneath it. items.reading_mnemonic: Kaa, the fire-breathing crow, dives straight down off the power line and lets out a sharp 「<reading>か</reading>」 as she plummets toward the ground below. Every time she drops down, that same caw of 「か」 rings out.
items.description: Means down or below; a very common kanji appearing in words about lower position, direction, and going down.

example_sentences.japanese: 本はあの窓の下です。
example_sentences.english: The book is under that window.
example_sentences.furigana: 本[ほん]はあの窓[まど]の下[した]です。

items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>person</radical> stands at the left with a line in his hand — you can see the <radical>barb</radical> at the end of it, and a flat bar of <radical>ground</radical> above the open <radical>mouth</radical> below. He has hooked something out of the water and hauled it up, and now he is just staring at it with his mouth hanging open, because he has no idea <radical>what</radical> it is.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kaa the fire-breathing crow drops onto the power line above him and looks at the thing on the hook. She has never seen one either. All she manages is one puzzled croak — 「<reading>か</reading>?」 — with a little puff of flame behind it. か? か? Neither of them knows.

example_sentences.japanese: これは何ですか。
example_sentences.english: What is this?
example_sentences.furigana: これは何[なに]ですか。

example_sentences.japanese: 今、何時ですか。

example_sentences.japanese: 朝ご飯に何を食べますか。
example_sentences.english: What will you eat for breakfast?
example_sentences.furigana: 朝[あさ]ご飯[はん]に何[なに]を食[た]べますか。

items.mnemonic_text: A box speared straight through the middle.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a <radical>mouth</radical>, that open square, and now imagine a single spear driven straight down through its center. The line splits the opening into two even halves, landing dead in the middle. Whatever you skewer that cleanly is right in the middle, tucked inside.
items.reading_mnemonic: Chuu, the loyal mouse, refuses to guard the door or the back — he plants himself squarely in the <reading>ちゅう</reading>, the very middle of the room, so no threat can slip past on either side. "The center is where a loyal mouse belongs," he squeaks.
items.description: Means middle or inside; extremely common, appearing in words about being in the middle of doing something, insides, and locations like the center of town.

example_sentences.japanese: みんな、中に入りました。
example_sentences.english: Everyone went inside.
example_sentences.furigana: みんな、中[なか]に入[はい]りました。

example_sentences.japanese: 部屋の真ん中に座りました。
example_sentences.english: I sat in the middle of the room.
example_sentences.furigana: 部屋[へや]の真[ま]ん中[なか]に座[すわ]りました。

example_sentences.japanese: 家の中で本を読みました。
example_sentences.english: I read a book inside the house.
example_sentences.furigana: 家[いえ]の中[なか]で本[ほん]を読[よ]みました。

items.mnemonic_text: A person stretching arms and legs out wide: big.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a person standing with their arms flung out and their legs spread as wide as they can go, straining to show you just how huge the fish they caught was. That whole stretched-out stick figure is this character. When someone stands like that, they're always telling you one thing: it was big.
items.reading_mnemonic: The person is stretching so wide because they're measuring Dai, the giant baby, who is the size of a truck. You gasp <reading>だい</reading> as he cries an earthquake and you realize nothing has ever been this big.
items.description: All four share the same spread-armed figure. 大 is the bare shape. 太 adds a dot underneath, 犬 adds a dot at the top right, and 天 caps it with an extra horizontal above the arms. If nothing has been added, it is 大.

example_sentences.japanese: その犬は大きいです。
example_sentences.english: That dog is big.
example_sentences.furigana: その犬[いぬ]は大[おお]きいです。

example_sentences.english: I am going to the university tomorrow.
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]、大[だい]学[がく]に行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: お母さんは大丈夫ですか。
example_sentences.english: Is your mother okay?
example_sentences.furigana: お母[かあ]さんは大[だい]丈[じょう]夫[ぶ]ですか。

items.mnemonic_text: Evening (夕) plus divination: reading fortunes outside.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The tortoise is out on the balcony again, squinting at the cracks in its shell, reading them by <radical>divination</radical>: clear tonight. So the hedgehog drags its fork out for another <radical>evening</radical> under the crescent moon. Neither is going back in yet. Both sit with the fence at their backs — firmly outside.
items.reading_mnemonic: You lock yourself out of Koichi's konbini after hours and a guy named Guy comes tapping the glass from the cold, calling "<reading>がい</reading>! I'm still stuck out here!" He is very much on the outside.
items.description: Means "outside"; a common N5 kanji appearing in words for the outdoors and things that are external.

example_sentences.japanese: 来年、外国に行きます。
example_sentences.english: Next year, I will go to a foreign country.
example_sentences.furigana: 来[らい]年[ねん]、外[がい]国[こく]に行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: あの人は外国人ですか。
example_sentences.english: Is that person a foreigner?
example_sentences.furigana: あの人[ひと]は外[がい]国[こく]人[じん]ですか。

example_sentences.japanese: 今日、外は寒いです。
example_sentences.english: It is cold outside today.
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]、外[そと]は寒[さむ]いです。

items.mnemonic_text: A blade cutting the way forward, in front of you.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a fancy storefront with a wide awning, and set into the wall a tall narrow window with two bars across it. The crescent <radical>moon</radical> has drifted down and wedged itself inside that frame, glowing like a display piece. It's there before the staff, before anyone — ahead of the whole shop. That shape is front, and before.
items.reading_mnemonic: A calm Zen monk stands out front of the shop, arriving before everyone else, and he bows and murmurs <reading>ぜん</reading> as he settles into place. He's always in ぜん — front and center, before the doors open.
items.description: Means front or before; extremely common in words for physical position (in front of) and time (before, previous), such as before an event or the front of a building.

example_sentences.japanese: ここに名前を書きます。
example_sentences.english: I will write my name here.
example_sentences.furigana: ここに名[な]前[まえ]を書[か]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 明日の午前、病院へ行きます。
example_sentences.english: I will go to the hospital tomorrow morning.
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]の午[ご]前[ぜん]、病[びょう]院[いん]へ行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 駅の前で友達を待ちます。
example_sentences.english: I will wait for my friend in front of the station.
example_sentences.furigana: 駅[えき]の前[まえ]で友[とも]達[だち]を待[ま]ちます。

items.mnemonic_text: A small step trailing behind: after and behind.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The penguin in the tipped hat takes one enormous sideways <radical>step</radical> across the buttered kitchen floor. A <radical>tiny thread</radical> is snagged on its heel, with the duckling tied to the far end. The duckling gets towed along as a permanent <radical>trailing foot</radical>, skidding a body-length back. Whatever the penguin does, the duckling comes after: behind.
items.reading_mnemonic: The trailing runner finally staggers across the finish line, dead last, and gasps out a weak "<reading>ご</reading>... ご..." — trying to say "go" but only managing to arrive after everyone else. That breathless ご is the sound that lands whenever this kanji shows up.

example_sentences.japanese: 駅の後ろで待ちます。
example_sentences.english: I will wait behind the station.
example_sentences.furigana: 駅[えき]の後[うし]ろで待[ま]ちます。

example_sentences.japanese: 今日の午後、図書館に行きます。
example_sentences.english: I will go to the library this afternoon.
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]の午[ご]後[ご]、図[と]書[しょ]館[かん]に行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: これが最後のお菓子です。
example_sentences.english: This is the last snack.
example_sentences.furigana: これが最[さい]後[ご]のお菓[か]子[し]です。

items.mnemonic_text: A marker at the top of the day: noon.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a sundial standing on the <radical>ground</radical> — that flat line is the earth beneath it. A pole rises up from the ground. At the top of the day, its shadow points straight down and vanishes onto that line. No shadow at all: that's exactly noon.
items.reading_mnemonic: At high noon a golfer named Gordon lines up his shot and yells "<reading>ご</reading>!" as he swings, because he can't wait until the sun drops. His voice echoes across the empty midday field: ご, ご, ご.
items.description: All three are bars on a vertical under a slanting flick. 午 has two bars and its vertical stops at the upper one. 牛 also has two, but its vertical pushes up above the top bar. 千 has only one bar.

example_sentences.japanese: 午前は学校に行きます。
example_sentences.english: I go to school in the morning.
example_sentences.furigana: 午[ご]前[ぜん]は学[がっ]校[こう]に行[い]きます。

example_sentences.furigana: 午[ご]後[ご]は映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ます。

example_sentences.japanese: 昨日の午前、友達に会いました。
example_sentences.english: I met a friend yesterday morning.
example_sentences.furigana: 昨日[きのう]の午[ご]前[ぜん]、友[とも]達[だち]に会[あ]いました。

items.mnemonic_text: A tree (木) with a line marking its root: the origin, a book.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a <radical>tree</radical> standing tall, with the <radical>ground</radical> drawn as one flat line across its trunk — right where the roots meet the soil. That line marks the tree's own origin. Press pages flat from that origin, and you have a book.
items.reading_mnemonic: A monk named <reading>ほん</reading> sits on the mossy steps at Grandma Kane's shrine, reading the same book over and over. Every time a cat brushes past, he mutters "ほん, ほん" without looking up — he cannot put that book down.
items.description: 本 is 木 with one extra stroke: a short horizontal laid across the lower trunk. Nothing else changes, so that little bar down at the base is the only thing to look for.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は毎日本を読みます。
example_sentences.english: I read a book every day.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は毎[まい]日本[にほん]を読[よ]みます。

example_sentences.japanese: 来年、日本に行きます。
example_sentences.english: I will go to Japan next year.
example_sentences.furigana: 来[らい]年[ねん]、日本[にほん]に行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 昨日はペンを三本買いました。
example_sentences.english: I bought three pens yesterday.
example_sentences.furigana: 昨日[きのう]はペンを三[さん]本[ぼん]買[か]いました。

items.mnemonic_text: Two legs walking: a person.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Look at the shape: two legs, mid-stride, walking forward and carrying nothing else along with them. That's the whole picture — a body up top, two legs striding out beneath. Two legs walking forward is a <radical>person</radical>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Jin, the friendly giant, is the biggest person you'll ever meet, ducking through every doorway just to say hello. When you spot this character, picture him waving down at you and hear the giant himself: <reading>じん</reading>.
items.description: 人 is the two-stroke figure that meets at a single clean peak. 入 slides its short stroke down the long one so the top overhangs, and 八 keeps the two strokes apart with a gap between them.

example_sentences.japanese: あの人は誰ですか。
example_sentences.english: Who is that person over there?
example_sentences.furigana: あの人[ひと]は誰[だれ]ですか。

example_sentences.japanese: 私の友達は外国人です。
example_sentences.english: My friend is a foreigner.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]の友[とも]達[だち]は外[がい]国[こく]人[じん]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 今日は一人で帰ります。
example_sentences.english: I will go home alone today.
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]は一人[ひとり]で帰[かえ]ります。

items.mnemonic_text: A figure kneeling gracefully: a woman.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Look closely at the character and you'll see a figure kneeling gracefully, one arm sweeping across, the other resting low. That elegant kneeling pose is exactly how you were taught to spot a <radical>woman</radical>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A woman named Jo sweeps into Koichi's konbini and orders in a booming voice, "<reading>じょ</reading>, that's me!" The whole shelf of onigiri rattles as she says it, so じょ is stuck to this woman for good.
items.description: Means "woman"; a very common N5 kanji that appears in words for females and in compounds relating to girls and women.

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女と一緒に映画館へ行きました。
example_sentences.english: I went to the cinema with my girlfriend.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]と一[いっ]緒[しょ]に映[えい]画[が]館[かん]へ行[い]きました。

example_sentences.japanese: あの女の人は誰ですか。
example_sentences.english: Who is that woman?
example_sentences.furigana: あの女[おんな]の人[ひと]は誰[だれ]ですか。

example_sentences.english: A girl is playing in the park.
example_sentences.furigana: 女[おんな]の子[こ]が公[こう]園[えん]で遊[あそ]んでいます。

items.mnemonic_text: A swaddled baby with arms out: a child.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Look closely at this character: it's a swaddled baby with its little arms flung out to the sides. That bundled shape wriggling and reaching is exactly what this kanji is — a <radical>child</radical>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A child at the riverbank keeps splashing everyone, so you press a finger to your lips and go "<reading>し</reading>!" — the sound you make to shush a rowdy kid. That soft "し" is how you hush this child.
items.description: Means "child"; a very common kanji appearing in words for children and as a frequent name ending.

example_sentences.english: That boy is my younger brother.
example_sentences.furigana: あの男[おとこ]の子[こ]は私[わたし]の弟[おとうと]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女は新しい帽子を買いました。
example_sentences.english: She bought a new hat.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は新[あたら]しい帽[ぼう]子[し]を買[か]いました。

example_sentences.japanese: 毎日、子供とお菓子を食べます。
example_sentences.english: I eat sweets with my child every day.
example_sentences.furigana: 毎[まい]日[にち]、子[こ]供[ども]とお菓[か]子[し]を食[た]べます。

items.mnemonic_text: An open square: a mouth.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Look at this character: it's just an open square, a hole with nothing inside. Picture it as a <radical>mouth</radical> hanging wide open, mid-yawn or mid-shout. An open square, an opening — a mouth.
items.reading_mnemonic: Koichi, the konbini king, leans across the beeping till and shouts an order to his stock boy, his mouth wide open: 「<reading>こう</reading>!」 Every time he barks like that, you picture that gaping mouth and hear こう.
items.description: Means "mouth" or "opening"; a common N5 kanji that shows up in words about mouths, entrances, and exits.

example_sentences.japanese: 赤ちゃんの口は小さいです。
example_sentences.english: The baby's mouth is small.
example_sentences.furigana: 赤[あか]ちゃんの口[くち]は小[ちい]さいです。

example_sentences.english: Where is the exit?
example_sentences.furigana: 出[で]口[ぐち]はどこですか。

example_sentences.japanese: 銀行の窓口に行きます。
example_sentences.english: I will go to the bank's service window.
example_sentences.furigana: 銀[ぎん]行[こう]の窓[まど]口[ぐち]に行[い]きます。

items.mnemonic_text: Fingers and a wrist branching out: a hand.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Look closely and you can see the fingers spreading out from a wrist. That's the whole picture: fingers plus a wrist, held up for you to shake. It's a <radical>hand</radical>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A magician named Shu reaches out a bare hand and, with a flick, pulls a coin from behind your ear. As the coin lands in her palm she winks and says, "<reading>しゅ</reading>, that's all in the hand."
items.description: Means "hand"; a very common kanji that appears in everyday words for hands, gestures, and doing things by hand.

example_sentences.english: His hands are big.

example_sentences.english: I bought a stamp at the post office.
example_sentences.furigana: 郵[ゆう]便[びん]局[きょく]で切[きっ]手[て]を買[か]いました。

items.mnemonic_text: A sprout pushing up from the ground: life and birth.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a single seed pushed into the <radical>earth</radical> — that cross of soil where everything begins. A green shoot cracks through and reaches up out of the ground. From that patch of earth, something new is born: this is life.
items.reading_mnemonic: Sei, the star student, is the first sprout to shoot up every spring, hand raised before anyone else has even woken. When the teacher asks who's most full of life, Sei（<reading>せい</reading>）is already standing, beaming.
items.description: Means "life" or "birth"; a very common kanji that shows up in words about living, being born, students, and fresh or raw things.

example_sentences.japanese: 昨日、駅で先生に会いました。
example_sentences.english: I met my teacher at the station yesterday.
example_sentences.furigana: 昨日[きのう]、駅[えき]で先[せん]生[せい]に会[あ]いました。

example_sentences.japanese: 学生は毎日図書館で本を読みます。

example_sentences.furigana: 去[きょ]年[ねん]、妹[いもうと]が生[う]まれました。

items.mnemonic_text: In the evening (夕) you call out a mouth's (口) name.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Up on the balcony, the hedgehog is out with its fork again, watching the crescent get bitten away for the <radical>evening</radical>. It still can't remember what the thief is called. So it leans over the railing, opens its <radical>mouth</radical> wide, and yells the one word that fills the gap. An evening sky plus a mouth shouting into it — that gives you a name.
items.reading_mnemonic: A performer named Mei struts into Koichi's konbini and belts out "<reading>めい</reading>, that's my name, don't wear it out!" She spells it letter by letter until the whole shop knows exactly who she is.
items.description: 名 and 多 both start with the same slanted three-stroke piece. 名 finishes with a small closed box beneath it. 多 repeats that slanted piece a second time instead, so it is one shape stacked twice.

example_sentences.japanese: 先生の名前は何ですか。
example_sentences.english: What is the teacher's name?
example_sentences.furigana: 先[せん]生[せい]の名[な]前[まえ]は何[なに]ですか。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼は有名な医者です。
example_sentences.english: He is a famous doctor.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]は有[ゆう]名[めい]な医[い]者[しゃ]です。

example_sentences.japanese: あの映画は有名です。
example_sentences.english: That movie is famous.
example_sentences.furigana: あの映[えい]画[が]は有[ゆう]名[めい]です。

items.mnemonic_text: A person carrying grain across one full year.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The scarecrow in the field is propped up on a warrior's shield, that flat board left out in the sun until it is cracked and completely <radical>dry</radical>. It has stood there watching the rice grow, get harvested, and grow again, straight through the full turn of the seasons. One complete loop of that dry board's silent watch is a year.
items.reading_mnemonic: A tired farmer counts the passing seasons by taking a nap in the shade of that scarecrow each time the harvest ends. He mumbles "<reading>ねん</reading>、ねん" — like the sleepy sound of nodding off — once for every year that rolls by.
items.description: Means "year"; a very common kanji appearing in dates, ages, and words about time.

example_sentences.japanese: 去年、海に行きました。
example_sentences.english: I went to the sea last year.
example_sentences.furigana: 去[きょ]年[ねん]、海[うみ]に行[い]きました。

example_sentences.japanese: 今年、新しいパソコンを買います。
example_sentences.english: I will buy a new computer this year.
example_sentences.furigana: 今年[ことし]、新[あたら]しいパソコンを買[か]います。

example_sentences.japanese: 来年、兄は大学に行きます。
example_sentences.english: My older brother will go to university next year.
example_sentences.furigana: 来[らい]年[ねん]、兄[あに]は大[だい]学[がく]に行[い]きます。

items.mnemonic_text: The sun (日) at the temple (寺) marks the hour.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>sun</radical> climbs its window over the shrine to start a new <radical>day</radical>. Its shadow falls across a signpost hammered into the <radical>earth</radical>. Someone has laid a ruler flat in the soil beside it, thumb pinning it down. Every time the shadow creeps forward, it ticks off one more <radical>inch</radical>. Sun, post and ruler together turn plain dirt into a clock — that's how you measure time.
items.reading_mnemonic: A cheerful clockmaker named Jiro keeps every timepiece in Koichi's konbini ticking, and each hour on the hour he shouts "<reading>じ</reading>! じ!" as the alarms go off. Whenever you need to know the time, you listen for Jiro's じ.
items.description: Means time or hour, and shows up everywhere you talk about clock time and telling the hour.

example_sentences.japanese: 今は何時ですか。
example_sentences.english: What time is it now?
example_sentences.furigana: 今[いま]は何[なん]時[じ]ですか。

example_sentences.japanese: 新しい時計を買いました。
example_sentences.english: I bought a new watch.
example_sentences.furigana: 新[あたら]しい時計[とけい]を買[か]いました。

example_sentences.japanese: 時々友達と映画を見ます。
example_sentences.english: I sometimes watch movies with friends.
example_sentences.furigana: 時[とき]々[どき]友[とも]達[だち]と映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ます。

items.mnemonic_text: The sun (日) seen through a gate (門): the space in between.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a <radical>gate</radical> with its two swinging doors thrown open. Right in the gap between them, the <radical>sun</radical> is hanging low, filling the opening with light. That sliver of sun caught in the gate is the space between things — an interval, the gap between.
items.reading_mnemonic: A guard named Kan stands watch in that gateway, timing exactly how long the sun lingers in the gap. Every time the interval passes he shouts "<reading>かん</reading>!" and slams one door shut.
items.description: 間 and 聞 are the same gate frame with different contents. 間 sets 日, the sun, inside the gateway. 聞 stands an ear there instead. What is framed by the gate settles it every time.

example_sentences.japanese: 病院はデパートと駅の間です。
example_sentences.english: The hospital is between the department store and the station.
example_sentences.furigana: 病[びょう]院[いん]はデパートと駅[えき]の間[あいだ]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 二時間テレビを見ました。
example_sentences.english: I watched TV for two hours.
example_sentences.furigana: 二[に]時[じ]間[かん]テレビを見[み]ました。

example_sentences.japanese: 三週間待ちました。
example_sentences.english: I waited for three weeks.
example_sentences.furigana: 三[さん]週[しゅう]間[かん]待[ま]ちました。

items.mnemonic_text: The sun (日) with wings and birds: naming each day of the week.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You flip the calendar, and the <radical>sun</radical> sits bright at the edge, marking the day. Someone sweeps the rest of the square clean with a stiff-pronged <radical>broom</radical>, cat asleep across the top prong. Every morning the sun climbs, and the broom shoves yesterday off the grid. Each swept-and-sunned square gets its label: a named weekday.
items.reading_mnemonic: Yoko, exhausted, groans "no more, no more" as she crosses off day after day on the wall calendar. Every square she reaches she moans <reading>よう</reading>, よう, because to her every single weekday feels the same.

example_sentences.japanese: 水曜日にデパートで新しい靴を買います。
example_sentences.english: I will buy new shoes at the department store on Wednesday.
example_sentences.furigana: 水[すい]曜[よう]日[ひ]にデパートで新[あたら]しい靴[くつ]を買[か]います。

example_sentences.japanese: 金曜日の夜は楽しいです。
example_sentences.english: Friday night is fun.
example_sentences.furigana: 金[きん]曜[よう]日[ひ]の夜[よる]は楽[たの]しいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 日曜日に公園で本を読みます。
example_sentences.english: I read books in the park on Sundays.
example_sentences.furigana: 日[にち]曜[よう]日[ひ]に公[こう]園[えん]で本[ほん]を読[よ]みます。

items.mnemonic_text: A roof over a moment held in the hand: now.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You spot a <radical>person</radical> walking forward under a wide roof that shelters them from the rain. They don't dwell on where they've been or where they're headed — under that roof, in this exact spot, all that matters is the present moment. A person taking cover means: now.
items.reading_mnemonic: Right now, this very second, Koichi is slamming down onigiri prices at the konbini and yelling "<reading>こん</reading>!" like a battle cry to get you buying before the moment passes. Every time you hear こん, you know it means now, now, now.
items.description: 今 and 会 wear the same wide roof. Under it 今 has only a short stroke and a small hook. 会 packs a fuller body beneath the roof, with a horizontal bar and legs below it.

example_sentences.japanese: 今、私は忙しいです。
example_sentences.english: I am busy right now.
example_sentences.furigana: 今[いま]、私[わたし]は忙[いそが]しいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 今日、友達が家に来ます。
example_sentences.english: A friend is coming to my house today.
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]、友[とも]達[だち]が家[いえ]に来[き]ます。

example_sentences.japanese: 今週、映画を見ます。
example_sentences.english: I will watch a movie this week.
example_sentences.furigana: 今[こん]週[しゅう]、映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ます。

items.mnemonic_text: Making a lap around the calendar road: one week.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a boxy calendar page laid flat, with a winding <radical>road</radical> threading across it, square to square. You put your footsteps down and <radical>advance</radical> one box at a time. The road curves right back to where it started. One full loop around that grid — that's one week.
items.reading_mnemonic: A woman named Shu (<reading>しゅう</reading>) plans her whole week on that looping calendar path, and every seven days she sighs "しゅう, another one done!" as she starts the loop again. Hear her say しゅう each time the week resets.

example_sentences.japanese: 週末に友達と遊びます。
example_sentences.english: I play with my friends on the weekend.
example_sentences.furigana: 週[しゅう]末[まつ]に友[とも]達[だち]と遊[あそ]びます。

example_sentences.japanese: 来週は忙しいです。
example_sentences.english: I am busy next week.
example_sentences.furigana: 来[らい]週[しゅう]は忙[いそが]しいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 先週、新しい本を買いました。
example_sentences.english: I bought a new book last week.
example_sentences.furigana: 先[せん]週[しゅう]、新[あたら]しい本[ほん]を買[か]いました。

items.mnemonic_text: A person over a mother figure repeating every time.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A wind-up alarm clock is bolted to the pole outside the station. Every morning, that same <radical>mother</radical> leans out of the departing train window. She posts a forgotten lunchbox onto the pole and shouts reheating instructions over the ringing. Same train, same pole, same hour, without fail. That relentless repetition is exactly what this means: every.
items.reading_mnemonic: The clock belongs to Mai, who winds it every morning and shouts "My time!" as it rings. Hear her name <reading>まい</reading> as the sound that hammers home the routine — every day, まい, まい, まい.
items.description: Means "every" and shows up in common time words for recurring events, such as every day, every week, and every morning.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は毎日コーヒーを飲みます。
example_sentences.english: I drink coffee every day.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は毎[まい]日[にち]コーヒーを飲[の]みます。

example_sentences.japanese: 父は毎晩本を読みます。
example_sentences.english: My father reads a book every night.
example_sentences.furigana: 父[ちち]は毎[まい]晩[ばん]本[ほん]を読[よ]みます。

example_sentences.japanese: 毎月図書館に行きます。
example_sentences.english: I go to the library every month.
example_sentences.furigana: 毎[まい]月[つき]図[と]書[しょ]館[かん]に行[い]きます。

items.mnemonic_text: A shape split evenly down the middle: half.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Two matchsticks lie crossed on the counter, making that <radical>ten</radical> mark. A cleaver comes straight down through the middle. What's left is two legs, kicked out evenly, each side mirroring the other. Ten cut clean down the centre, split into equal parts — that's half.
items.reading_mnemonic: Han, the half-and-half chef, holds up a plate where one side is rice and the other is curry, split exactly down the center. "<reading>はん</reading>!" he barks, tapping the dividing line — because to Han, half is the only portion worth serving.
items.description: 半 and 羊 both sit horizontal bars on a vertical under a split top. Count the bars: 半 has two, 羊 has three. That extra horizontal is the only reliable difference.

example_sentences.japanese: 毎日二時間半勉強します。
example_sentences.english: I study for two and a half hours every day.
example_sentences.furigana: 毎[まい]日[にち]二[に]時[じ]間[かん]半[はん]勉[べん]強[きょう]します。

example_sentences.japanese: 私はこのパンを半分食べます。
example_sentences.english: I will eat half of this bread.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]はこのパンを半[はん]分[ぶん]食[た]べます。

example_sentences.japanese: 本の半分を読みました。
example_sentences.english: I read half of the book.
example_sentences.furigana: 本[ほん]の半[はん]分[ぶん]を読[よ]みました。

items.mnemonic_text: A sword (刀) dividing something into parts and minutes.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The woodcutter prises a chipped <radical>sword</radical> out of its frozen rice cake and wipes it clean. She gives it one job: split a log. It comes down clean, and the two halves lean apart into a fresh <radical>eight</radical>. One minute, one cut, and the sword finally earns its keep.
items.reading_mnemonic: The woodcutter, sawdust in her eyebrows, times herself at one log a minute and calls it the most <reading>fun</reading> you can have before breakfast. The sword, back in her hands and still chipped, snorts <reading>ふん</reading> — it was the one doing all the work.

example_sentences.japanese: この本は分かりません。
example_sentences.english: I don't understand this book.
example_sentences.furigana: この本[ほん]は分[わ]かりません。

example_sentences.japanese: パンを半分食べました。
example_sentences.english: I ate half of the bread.
example_sentences.furigana: パンを半[はん]分[ぶん]食[た]べました。

example_sentences.japanese: 駅で五分待ちました。
example_sentences.english: I waited for five minutes at the station.
example_sentences.furigana: 駅[えき]で五[ご]分[ふん]待[ま]ちました。

items.mnemonic_text: A child (子) under a roof of scattered ideas: study.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a swaddled <radical>child</radical>, arms out, parked under a low <radical>cover</radical> of scribbled notes. The cover tucks in at the edges like a blanket over a sleeping cat. All you hear is pencil scratching. A child kept all day under a canopy of lessons — that's study, that's learning.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the school, the star pupil Gaku is the one who never stops studying, and everyone in the echoing hallways calls out <reading>がく</reading> whenever they need the answer. Hear がく and you hear the kid who lives to learn.
items.description: Means study or learning; a very common kanji that shows up in words for student, school, and academic subjects.

example_sentences.japanese: 妹は学生です。
example_sentences.english: My younger sister is a student.
example_sentences.furigana: 妹[いもうと]は学[がく]生[せい]です。

example_sentences.japanese: 明日、学校に行きます。
example_sentences.english: I will go to school tomorrow.
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]、学[がっ]校[こう]に行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 数学は難しいです。
example_sentences.english: Math is difficult.
example_sentences.furigana: 数[すう]学[がく]は難[むずか]しいです。

items.mnemonic_text: A person stepping ahead of the rest: previous and first.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You spot two <radical>legs</radical> left standing without a body, striding out the door ahead of everyone else. No torso to slow them down — those legs are always one step in front, gone before you've even moved. Whatever they're doing, they did it previous to you and they're already ahead.
items.reading_mnemonic: Those bodiless legs sprint down the mountain trail so far ahead they trip a wire and set off a whole line of fireworks — <reading>せん</reading>, せん, せん — bursting one after another to mark how far in front they already are.

example_sentences.japanese: 昨日、先生に会いました。
example_sentences.english: I met the teacher yesterday.
example_sentences.furigana: 昨日[きのう]、先[せん]生[せい]に会[あ]いました。

example_sentences.japanese: 先週、友達と一緒に映画を見ました。
example_sentences.english: I watched a movie with a friend last week.
example_sentences.furigana: 先[せん]週[しゅう]、友[とも]達[だち]と一[いっ]緒[しょ]に映[えい]画[が]を見[み]ました。

example_sentences.japanese: 先月、新しい靴を買いました。
example_sentences.english: I bought new shoes last month.
example_sentences.furigana: 先[せん]月[げつ]、新[あたら]しい靴[くつ]を買[か]いました。

items.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>sun</radical> on the left, and on the right a <radical>stick</radical> driven upright into the dirt with one stroke that <radical>slides</radical> off it. That stick is a sundial, and the shadow it threw is still scratched into the ground beside it. The sun has moved on. The mark it left behind belongs to <radical>yesterday</radical>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Saku is the old gardener who checks his shadow-stick every dawn and then grumbles about how much better the light was 「<reading>さく</reading>」 — his one-word shorthand for the day before. Nothing is ever as good as さく was.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は昨日図書館で本を読みました。
example_sentences.english: I read a book at the library yesterday.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は昨日[きのう]図[と]書[しょ]館[かん]で本[ほん]を読[よ]みました。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼女は一昨日友達に会いました。
example_sentences.english: She met a friend the day before yesterday.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かの]女[じょ]は一[いっ]昨[さく]日[ひ]友[とも]達[だち]に会[あ]いました。

example_sentences.japanese: 昨日の朝、公園で犬と遊びました。
example_sentences.english: Yesterday morning, I played with a dog in the park.
example_sentences.furigana: 昨日[きのう]の朝[あさ]、公[こう]園[えん]で犬[いぬ]と遊[あそ]びました。

items.mnemonic_text: Speech (言) plus a tongue (舌): telling a story.
items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>mouth</radical> releasing stacked lines of <radical>speech</radical> leans in close, and right beside it a <radical>tongue</radical> sticks out of a mouth, wagging nonstop. Put the speech next to the busy tongue and you've got someone who just won't stop talking, spinning story after story.
items.reading_mnemonic: Wanda the storyteller loves an audience, so she waves both hands and calls out "<reading>わ</reading>!" every time she starts a new tale. That little "わ" is her signal that another long talk is about to begin.
items.description: Means talk or story; shows up in everyday words for speaking, conversation, and telephone.

example_sentences.japanese: 明日、友達と話します。
example_sentences.english: I will talk with my friend tomorrow.
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]、友[とも]達[だち]と話[はな]します。

example_sentences.japanese: 新しい電話を買いました。
example_sentences.english: I bought a new phone.
example_sentences.furigana: 新[あたら]しい電[でん]話[わ]を買[か]いました。

example_sentences.japanese: 先生の話は面白いです。
example_sentences.english: The teacher's story is interesting.
example_sentences.furigana: 先[せん]生[せい]の話[はなし]は面[おも]白[しろ]いです。

items.mnemonic_text: The sun (日) beside the moon (月): both lighting up, bright.
items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, two windows glow in the mossy wall at dawn. Through one climbs the blazing <radical>sun</radical>, starting the day. Through the other hangs the pale <radical>moon</radical>, refusing to set. Sun and moon blaze through both windows at once, flooding the courtyard until the cats squint. This is bright.
items.reading_mnemonic: Outside the gate stands a tourist named May, camera raised at the blinding courtyard. She keeps muttering <reading>めい</reading>, <reading>May</reading>, hunting for the word for bright and finding only her own name, so she just points at the glare instead.

example_sentences.japanese: 明日、友達と公園に行きます。
example_sentences.english: Tomorrow I'm going to the park with a friend.
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]、友[とも]達[だち]と公[こう]園[えん]に行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: この部屋はとても明るいです。
example_sentences.english: This room is very bright.
example_sentences.furigana: この部屋[へや]はとても明[あか]るいです。

example_sentences.japanese: 先生が問題を説明しました。
example_sentences.english: The teacher explained the problem.
example_sentences.furigana: 先[せん]生[せい]が問[もん]題[だい]を説[せつ]明[めい]しました。

items.mnemonic_text: A brush (聿) laid over a sunny page: writing.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>brush</radical> is back on your desk, still flecked with ink from the certificate it ruined. You dip it as the <radical>sun</radical> — that window with a bar in it — sinks below the edge of your notebook. Its last light lies flat across the page. Line after line goes down under that glow, until the whole <radical>day</radical> sits on paper. Sun on the page, brush in your fist: that is write.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kaa, the fire-breathing crow, lands on your notebook and squints at your terrible handwriting, muttering "<reading>しょ</reading>, しょ" every time you smudge a letter. Each little puff of flame dries the ink so you can keep writing.
items.description: Means "write"; shows up in words about writing, documents, and books, like 書く (to write).

example_sentences.japanese: 図書館で本を読みます。
example_sentences.english: I will read a book at the library.
example_sentences.furigana: 図[と]書[しょ]館[かん]で本[ほん]を読[よ]みます。

example_sentences.japanese: 友達に手紙を書きました。
example_sentences.english: I wrote a letter to a friend.
example_sentences.furigana: 友[とも]達[だち]に手[て]紙[がみ]を書[か]きました。

example_sentences.japanese: かばんに辞書を入れました。
example_sentences.english: I put the dictionary in my bag.
example_sentences.furigana: かばんに辞[じ]書[しょ]を入[い]れました。

items.mnemonic_text: An ear (耳) inside the gate (門): listening for who is there.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You press your <radical>ear</radical> right up against a <radical>gate</radical> to catch the whispers on the other side. The wood is cold, but you hold still, straining that one ear against the swinging doors. When you press an ear to a gate like this, you're doing two things at once: you hear, and you're dying to ask what's going on.
items.reading_mnemonic: Mon-Bun, the scholarly rabbit twins, press their ears to the gate to hear you ask a question — and immediately start arguing about the answer. "<reading>ぶん</reading>!" they squeak in unison, because those two never agree on anything they overhear.
items.description: 聞 and 間 are the same gate frame with different things standing inside it. 聞 puts 耳, an ear, in the gateway. 間 frames the sun there instead. What the gate contains is the whole difference.

example_sentences.japanese: 毎朝ラジオを聞きます。
example_sentences.english: I listen to the radio every morning.
example_sentences.furigana: 毎[まい]朝[あさ]ラジオを聞[き]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 父は朝、新聞を読みます。
example_sentences.english: My father reads the newspaper in the morning.

example_sentences.japanese: 鳥の声が聞こえます。
example_sentences.english: I can hear birds singing.
example_sentences.furigana: 鳥[とり]の声[こえ]が聞[き]こえます。

items.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>sun</radical> is caught low in a <radical>cross</radical>-braced frame on the left, still climbing, while over on the right the <radical>moon</radical> has not gone down yet. Both of them are up there at once. That happens for about twenty minutes a day, and only ever at one end of it: <radical>morning</radical>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Chou is the long-distance runner who is out before anybody else, and she stretches her greeting the whole length of the street as she passes your window — a long, unreasonably cheerful 「<reading>ちょう</reading>」. If you hear ちょう, the moon is still up.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は毎朝六時に起きます。
example_sentences.english: I get up at six every morning.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は毎[まい]朝[あさ]六[ろく]時[じ]に起[お]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 朝ご飯にパンを食べます。
example_sentences.english: I eat bread for breakfast.
example_sentences.furigana: 朝[あさ]ご飯[はん]にパンを食[た]べます。

example_sentences.japanese: 朝、公園で犬と遊びます。
example_sentences.english: In the morning, I play with the dog in the park.
example_sentences.furigana: 朝[あさ]、公[こう]園[えん]で犬[いぬ]と遊[あそ]びます。

items.mnemonic_text: A crossroads where you choose to go.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a stick figure caught mid-stride, legs split wide, one arm swinging forward — the whole character leans into the <radical>step</radical>. That's a person who won't stand still, always moving to the next place. When you see this shape, you see someone about to go.
items.reading_mnemonic: Koichi, the konbini king, can't sit still either — the second a shelf goes empty he's out the door to go restock it, muttering "<reading>こう</reading>, こう, keep it moving." Wherever he needs to go, he goes at a run.
items.description: Means "go" and shows up constantly in verbs of movement and travel, such as 行く (to go).

example_sentences.japanese: 昨日、銀行に行きました。
example_sentences.english: Yesterday, I went to the bank.
example_sentences.furigana: 昨日[きのう]、銀[ぎん]行[こう]に行[い]きました。

example_sentences.japanese: 家族と飛行機で旅行します。
example_sentences.english: I will travel by airplane with my family.
example_sentences.furigana: 家[か]族[ぞく]と飛[ひ]行[こう]機[き]で旅[りょ]行[こう]します。

example_sentences.japanese: お母さん、行ってきます。
example_sentences.english: I'm off, Mom.
example_sentences.furigana: お母[かあ]さん、行[い]ってきます。

items.meaning_mnemonic: A <radical>body</radical> is slumped across the top with a single <radical>drop</radical> of sweat coming off it, and directly underneath sits the <radical>sun</radical>, pinned against a flat line of <radical>ground</radical>. It is straight overhead and there is no shade left anywhere. Work has stopped and everyone has lain down. This is the flattening middle of the <radical>daytime</radical>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Chuu the loyal mouse will not nap through it. While every other body is flat out he stands at his post in the full sun, squeaking 「<reading>ちゅう</reading>」 on the hour so that nobody oversleeps. Absurdly devoted, ちゅう, right through the worst of it.

example_sentences.japanese: 私は毎日昼ご飯を食べます。
example_sentences.english: I eat lunch every day.
example_sentences.furigana: 私[わたし]は毎[まい]日[にち]昼[ひる]ご飯[はん]を食[た]べます。

example_sentences.japanese: 彼とは昼頃会いました。
example_sentences.english: I met him around noon.
example_sentences.furigana: 彼[かれ]とは昼[ひる]頃[ころ]会[あ]いました。

example_sentences.japanese: 今日の昼ご飯はパンでした。
example_sentences.english: Today's lunch was bread.
example_sentences.furigana: 今日[きょう]の昼[ひる]ご飯[はん]はパンでした。

items.mnemonic_text: A tree of grain drawing people to come.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture a <radical>tree</radical> standing at a crossroads with two little travelers resting under its branches, one on each side of the trunk. The tree can't move, so it waves the travelers over: "Come! Come to me, sit in my shade." Everyone always comes to the tree.
items.reading_mnemonic: The traveler who comes to the tree is Rye, and he never arrives quietly — he shouts "<reading>らい</reading>, I'm here!" as he strolls up the path. Whenever someone comes into view down the road, listen for that らい.
items.description: 来 is 米 with an extra horizontal across the top. Count the horizontal bars: 米 has one, 来 has two.

example_sentences.japanese: 明日、誰が来ますか。
example_sentences.english: Who is coming tomorrow?
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]、誰[だれ]が来[き]ますか。

example_sentences.japanese: 来月、日本へ行きます。
example_sentences.english: I will go to Japan next month.
example_sentences.furigana: 来[らい]月[げつ]、日本[にほん]へ行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 来年、新しい先生が来ます。
example_sentences.english: A new teacher will come next year.
example_sentences.furigana: 来[らい]年[ねん]、新[あたら]しい先[せん]生[せい]が来[き]ます。

items.mnemonic_text: A flag on a pole pointing a direction.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture 方 as one warped signpost bolted into a crossroads. Its crossbar arm won't hold still — it spins in the wind until it locks facing one <radical>direction</radical>, and a lost traveler grabs the swinging arm just to have something to follow. One pole, one direction, and the person now walking it.
items.reading_mnemonic: An owl called <reading>Hoot</reading> lands on the swinging signpost's crossbar and states the obvious in one flat call, <reading>ほう</reading>, every single time the arm swings past true north.
items.description: 万 is simpler than it looks: one long horizontal capped by a single sweeping curve that swings down and left into a hook, nothing above it. 方 carries an extra short tick above its crossbar before the vertical stroke kicks left and hooks at the bottom — that top tick is the tell. No tick, it's 万; tick present, it's 方.

example_sentences.japanese: 夕方に公園を散歩します。

example_sentences.japanese: この方法は易しいです。
example_sentences.english: This method is easy.
example_sentences.furigana: この方[ほう]法[ほう]は易[やさ]しいです。

example_sentences.japanese: あの方はとても親切です。
example_sentences.english: That person over there is very kind.
example_sentences.furigana: あの方[ほう]はとても親[しん]切[せつ]です。

items.mnemonic_text: A broom and a stop: sweeping up and returning home.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You push your own front door open, and the <radical>broom</radical> is still sweeping crumbs down the hallway — same as you left it this morning. The cat gives up and burrows under its <radical>cover</radical> on the porch. Your <radical>cloth</radical> still hangs on the hook in two limp folds. You take it down and wipe the day off your face. Coming back to the same broom, blanket and cloth — that's what it is to return.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kiki, the tree spirit, has been out riding the wind all day, and now she giggles as she slips back inside her old tree with a soft <reading>き</reading>. Watch her return home and you'll hear that き every time.
items.description: Means "return," as in going or coming back home; the core kanji in the verb 帰る, to return.

example_sentences.japanese: 明日は早く家に帰ります。
example_sentences.english: I will return home early tomorrow.
example_sentences.furigana: 明日[あした]は早[はや]く家[いえ]に帰[かえ]ります。

example_sentences.furigana: お父[とう]さん、お帰[かえ]りなさい。

items.meaning_mnemonic: The <radical>sun</radical> on the left has finally been let off: the shape on the right is the one that squeezes out from under the heavy lid and walks away <radical>exempt</radical>. Its shift is done, it has clocked out, and it drops below the roofline without waiting to be dismissed. The sun excused from duty is <radical>nightfall</radical>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Ban is the night watchman who takes over the moment the sun clocks off. He drags the gate shut and announces himself to the empty street — 「<reading>ばん</reading>」 — one flat syllable, every night, so you know the day is closed.

example_sentences.furigana: 晩[ばん]ご飯[はん]はレストランで食[た]べましょう。

items.mnemonic_text: Two mountains stacked, something pushing out.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Look closely and you see one <radical>mountain</radical> stacked right on top of another mountain — two sets of three peaks piled up. When the peaks get that tall, there's only one thing you want to do: get out and leave. So this doubled-up mountain means exit, leave.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the exit of the mountain trail stands a hiker who sneezes so hard every time someone leaves — a huge "<reading>しゅつ</reading>!" — that the whole vending machine rattles. Every time you head for the exit, you hear that "しゅつ" behind you.
items.description: Means exit or leave; shows up in everyday words about going out, leaving, and departures.

example_sentences.japanese: 明日、手紙を出します。

items.mnemonic_text: A person ducking under a doorway to enter.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Watch the shape closely: it's a little figure ducking their head as they pass under a low doorway. You lean, you dip, you step through — and just like that, you <radical>enter</radical>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The figure ducking through the door is a new student, and as they enter the echoing school hallway everyone whispers "the new one, <reading>にゅう</reading>, the new one." Every time someone new enters, that にゅう ripples down the hall.
items.description: 入, 人 and 八 are the same pair of strokes. In 入 the short left stroke begins partway down the long one, leaving a small overhang at the top. 人 meets at a clean point, and 八 never lets the two touch.

example_sentences.japanese: 友達と一緒に店に入りました。

example_sentences.japanese: 駅の入口はどこですか。

example_sentences.furigana: 駅[えき]の入[いり]口[ぐち]はどこですか。

items.mnemonic_text: An eye (目) on legs going out to see.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Take an <radical>eye</radical> (目) and stand it up on a pair of <radical>human legs</radical> (儿), and suddenly it can walk around anywhere it wants. Where does an eye on legs go? Out into the world, to look at everything. So this is what it means to <radical>see</radical>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Ken, the sword-collecting dog, drags you over to his wall of antique swords because he wants you to see his newest one. "<reading>けん</reading>! けん!" he barks, pawing at the blade until you finally look.
items.description: Means "see" and is the base of the common verb 見る (to see/look); it shows up constantly in everyday words about looking and watching.

example_sentences.japanese: 毎日テレビを見ます。

example_sentences.furigana: 毎[まい]日[にち]テレビを見[み]ます。

example_sentences.japanese: 友達に新しい写真を見せました。

example_sentences.furigana: 友[とも]達[だち]に新[あたら]しい写[しゃ]真[しん]を見[み]せました。

items.mnemonic_text: A net (罒) over money (貝): buying with cash.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You spot something you want, so you reach for the cowrie <radical>shell</radical> that once worked as money. You lay that shell on the counter and slide it across. Handing over the shell-money is how you buy.
items.reading_mnemonic: The moment you buy your onigiri at Koichi's konbini, Kaa the fire-breathing crow swoops in and shrieks 「<reading>ばい</reading>」 as if saying "bye-bye" to your cash before you've even paid.
items.description: Means "buy," the verb 買う (to purchase); shows up constantly in shopping and everyday transactions.

example_sentences.english: I bought a new book yesterday.

items.mnemonic_text: A roof over a heap of good rice: food to eat.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Look at the whole character as a little tent pitched over a full table: the peaked roof on top, and underneath it a heaped tray of rice and side dishes. It's the family shelter you duck into when you're hungry — a roof made entirely of dinner. Under that roof there's only one thing to do: eat the food.
items.reading_mnemonic: A cheerful line cook at Koichi's konbini slings hot lunches under the fluorescent lights, and every time a tray lands he shouts his catchphrase: <reading>しょく</reading>, しょく, come and get it! You hear しょく and your stomach knows it's time to eat.
items.description: Means eat or food; shows up in everyday words for meals, eating, and food, and as the verb "to eat."

example_sentences.furigana: どんな食[た]べ物[もの]が好[す]きですか。

items.mnemonic_text: A ray of sunlight so bright it turns white.
items.meaning_mnemonic: You step outside Koichi's konbini and the morning sun hits you full in the face — a ray of light so bright everything goes pure <radical>white</radical> for a second. You blink, and the whole world is still washed out and white. That blinding ray is your picture for white.
items.reading_mnemonic: The dazzling light spooks a startled hawk perched on the konbini roof; it beats its wings once and goes, <reading>はく</reading>, hacking out a cough as it flaps into the too-bright sky. Hear that はく every time you see this pure white flash.
items.description: All four are the same box with bars inside, and the top settles it. 白 caps the box with a small flick. 百 turns that cap into a full-width horizontal. 自 uses a short slash instead. 日 has no cap at all.

example_sentences.furigana: その白[しろ]い靴[くつ]は新[あたら]しいですか。

items.mnemonic_text: The earth glowing under a big fire: red.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the ground cracking open on the mountain trail, and underneath it the Earth is glowing — lit from below by a fire you can't see. That heat pushes up through the soil until the whole hillside burns a deep, angry <radical>red</radical>. Earth glowing under a fire: red.
items.reading_mnemonic: The guy who lit that underground fire is Seki, and he's coughing his lungs out from the smoke — a wet, rattling <reading>せき</reading> that won't stop as long as the red embers keep burning. Every time he sees red he starts up again: せき, せき, せき.
items.description: Means "red"; a common color kanji that shows up in words for the color itself and things like traffic lights.

items.mnemonic_text: A sooty village over a fire: black with smoke.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture the whole <radical>village</radical> at dusk, huddled around one big cooking fire. Smoke climbs and stains every wall. It settles over the paddies, the packed earth, the wooden houses. The sooty village standing over that fire has turned one single colour: <radical>black</radical>.
items.reading_mnemonic: The soot-covered villagers cough up thick black lungfuls, hacking <reading>こく</reading>, こく into the night air. Every cough is darker than the last — that's the sound of black.
items.description: Means "black"; the everyday word for the color (くろ) and a common on'yomi こく in compounds.

items.mnemonic_text: Two evenings (夕) stacked: many days piling up.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The hedgehog is back on the balcony with its fork, watching the crescent get bitten away for the <radical>evening</radical>, when a second <radical>evening</radical> stacks up underneath the first, leaning like a lopsided snowman. One moon is never enough. It wants another, and another, until the plate is piled high. Two stacked and still craving more: that is how you get many.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the top of the mountain trail, Ta counts the coins in the improbable vending machine, and there are far too many to hold. "<reading>た</reading>, た, た," she taps each one as they spill from her hands — there are just too many.
items.description: 多 is the same slanted piece written twice, one stacked below the other. 名 writes that piece once and puts a small closed box underneath it instead.

items.mnemonic_text: A jewel (玉) enclosed by borders: a country.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Picture an <radical>enclosure</radical>, a closed box with walls around everything inside, and set the <radical>jewel</radical> — that skewered stack of crowns, gems and all — down in the middle of it. Draw those walls big enough and you're no longer fencing a garden; you're fencing a whole people in around their crown. Walls wrapped around a king give you a country.
items.reading_mnemonic: At the border of this walled country stands a guard named Koku, who stamps every passport with a cheerful <reading>こく</reading> sound. No stamp, no entry — こく, こく, all day long.
items.description: Means "country" or "nation"; a very common kanji seen in words for countries and citizenship, read こく in compounds and くに on its own.

items.mnemonic_text: Rain (雨) with lightning stretching down: electricity.

Every plot lights up at once — the whole grid crackles with electricity.
items.reading_mnemonic: The lightning hits a power line and the whole street goes DEN — <reading>でん</reading> — every fluorescent tube in Koichi's konbini surging bright at once. You feel that でん in your teeth as the electricity floods back.
items.description: Means "electricity"; shows up in everyday words for trains, phones, lights, and anything electrical.

items.mnemonic_text: A cart seen from above with an axle: a vehicle.
items.meaning_mnemonic: Look straight down at a cart from above: one long axle running through the middle, wheels flanking each side, a boxy frame around it all. That's exactly what this character is — a cart seen from overhead with its axle drawn right through it. Trace that shape and you're looking at a <radical>vehicle</radical>.
items.reading_mnemonic: A show-off racer revs his engine outside Koichi's konbini and shouts "Watch me!" — but he peels out so fast all you hear is a screech of "<reading>しゃ</reading>!" as the vehicle vanishes down the street. Every time you see this car kanji, that "しゃ!" is the last sound it makes.
items.description: 車 and 重 are the same boxy stack, but 重 is taller and runs an extra horizontal through the middle. Count the horizontal strokes crossing the body: 重 always has one more than 車.

example_sentences.japanese: 毎朝電車で会社に行きます。
example_sentences.english: Every morning I take the train to the office.
example_sentences.furigana: 毎[まい]朝[あさ]電[でん]車[しゃ]で会[かい]社[しゃ]に行[い]きます。

items.mnemonic_text: A roof over a pig (豕): the traditional house.
items.meaning_mnemonic: The pigeon sliding belly-first down that slick <radical>roof</radical> shoots off the eaves and through an open window, landing on the <radical>pig</radical> mid belly-rub, legs already kicking the air in outrage. Pig and pigeon end up tangled on one floor under one roof — and a roof with a pig living underneath, indignities and all, is what makes a house a house.
items.reading_mnemonic: Kaa the fire-breathing crow perches on the power line outside that house, unimpressed by the racket inside. Every time the pig squeals and kicks at the ceiling, she tips her head back and lets out one flat <reading>か</reading> — a dry little <reading>kah</reading> of judgment, then goes back to smoking her own beak.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Two arms crossing over each other at the top, two legs braced wide underneath. It is a stance, not a face — the shape of a man standing square in a doorway with his arms folded, filling the whole frame, waiting to hear what you have got to say for yourself. Everybody recognises that silhouette: <radical>father</radical>.
items.reading_mnemonic: Fu is the long breath out through the nose that he gives you instead of an answer — 「<reading>ふ</reading>」 — arms still folded. Not angry. Not pleased either. Just ふ, and you will be hearing it for the rest of your life.

example_sentences.japanese: 父は毎日忙しいです。
example_sentences.english: My father is busy every day.
example_sentences.furigana: 父[ちち]は毎[まい]日[にち]忙[いそが]しいです。

example_sentences.japanese: お父さんは今日会社に行きます。
example_sentences.english: Father is going to the office today.
example_sentences.furigana: お父[とう]さんは今日[きょう]会[かい]社[しゃ]に行[い]きます。

example_sentences.japanese: 祖父は公園で犬と遊びます。
example_sentences.english: My grandfather plays with the dog at the park.
example_sentences.furigana: 祖[そ]父[ふ]は公[こう]園[えん]で犬[いぬ]と遊[あそ]びます。

items.meaning_mnemonic: A figure kneeling with her arms wrapped round in front of her, and two dots marking the breasts that fed you. The entire character is built around those two points; take them out and it turns into a different word altogether. They are the reason the shape exists at all, and the reason you call her <radical>mother</radical>.

items.mnemonic_text: A woman (女) who is already (市-like) senior: the older sister.

She drapes a folded <radical>cloth</radical> over her shoulders like a cape, then rams a <radical>lid</radical> onto her head as a makeshift hat. She marches off, ordering the younger kids about their washing. That swaggering, self-appointed supervisor is your older sister.
items.reading_mnemonic: Back at the river, she silences the squabbling kids with one sharp <reading>し</reading> — a hissed <reading>shh</reading> that cuts through the splashing instantly — the unmistakable sound of an older sister taking charge.
items.description: Don't confuse this with 妹, the kanji for younger sister. Here the right side stacks a lid over a hanging fold of cloth, a cap over drapery. In 妹 the right side is a tree with an extra short stroke near the top, giving two branches instead of one. Cap-over-cloth is older; two branches is younger.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At Grandma Kane's shrine, you grab the frayed rope and swing the huge bell for the first time in your life. The clapper catches wrong, and instead of a clean toll it screeches like a rusty gate, sending every cat on the mossy steps bolting off at once. That flinching, unrepeatable racket is what a first time actually sounds like.
items.reading_mnemonic: Still ringing in your ears, the shrine's fattest cat gives one hoarse, botched yowl — not a full meow, just a wheezy <reading>しょ</reading>, like a magician trying to <reading>show</reading> off a trick that didn't land. Every disastrous first attempt at that bell gets remembered by that one broken sound.

items.meaning_mnemonic: Sei's school has exactly one door at the end of the main hallway, its hand-lettered plaque nailed on crooked, at an angle no carpenter would allow. Every subject in the building — science, math, home ec — funnels through that single lopsided doorway, because nobody built a second one. That one overloaded, off-kilter door is the department.

The cough comes out hoarse and flat, <reading>か</reading>, like a stalling <reading>car</reading> engine — the sound the school now associates with that overworked door.

items.meaning_mnemonic: At the very top of the mountain trail, past where the vending machine has any business being, one hiker drops face-first onto the last flat rock before the ground falls away.
